rules: Students must have a minimum overall GPA of 3.5.
Students enrolled in an AP course must earn a semester grade no lower than a B (80 or higher) in that course to remain in that department's AP-level track the following year.
Students in an honors-level course must earn a semester grade no lower than an A (90 or above) to move up to that department's AP-level course the following year.
AP courses require semester exams and the AP test in the subject, at additional expense, with the possibility of earning college credit.
Course offerings are subject to the availability of an instructor and sufficient student enrollment.
Students already in an Honors course must achieve a semester grade of B (80+) in the prerequisite course(s) to remain in that department's Honors level the following year.
Students in a College Prep course must achieve a semester grade of A (90+) in the prerequisite course(s) to move up to that department's Honors level the following year.
Dual enrollment courses for credit through St. Thomas University are offered on campus.
Students must have at least a 3.0 GPA to register for a dual enrollment course.
Payment for dual enrollment courses is due at the beginning of the school year or semester.

course_credit_policies: All students take six classes each semester.
Credit for all classes is awarded by semester (0.5 credits).
A student will not be promoted to the next grade unless all previous credits have been earned.
A student who fails a semester in any course is required to remediate that course immediately; remediation classes are offered in Spring and Summer sessions.
Students who receive a D are also strongly advised to remediate the course.

notes: Placement in courses for the following school year is based upon grades earned in the previous semester.
After re-registration and course selection, students receive a preliminary course list before the end of the school year, then have a one-week period to review it with their counselor.
Requests for course changes are not accepted once the master schedule has been created.
In rare instances where a class change is granted after the deadline, a fee applies after the schedule change form is completed by the guidance counselor.
Some schedule change requests cannot be granted due to conflicts with other courses.

registration_procedure: Using this guide or the course descriptions on Plus Portals, students plan their courses for the following school year.
Students complete the four-year planning sheet, verifying grade level and prerequisites for each course.
Parents / guardians receive a re-registration email from the school.
Students receive their transcript and a Plus Portals digital course selection link.
Students submit their Plus Portals digital course selection form, with the option of meeting with their counselor on assigned meeting dates.

Once the parent pays the registration fee, sets up a FACTS agreement, completes the student information form, and makes any necessary AP exam fee payments, the counselor finalizes the student's course requests.

notes: Every grade is assigned a specific number of quality points, depending upon the level of the course.
The simple GPA is used to determine athletic eligibility and does not include the additional points awarded for honors, dual enrollment, or AP courses.
Weighted courses are noted in this guide with asterisks.

courses.title: Faith and Revelation / Christology
courses.description: Semester 1 (Faith and Revelation): The purpose of this course is to give students a general knowledge and appreciation of the Sacred Scriptures. Through their study of the Bible, students will encounter the living Word of God, Jesus Christ. The course will teach students about the Bible, authored by God through Inspiration, and its value to people throughout the world. Students will learn how to read the Bible and become familiar with its major sections and books, paying particular attention to the Gospels. Semester 2 (Christology): The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the mystery of Jesus Christ, the living Word of God, the Second Person of the Blessed Trinity. Students will be taught to understand that Jesus Christ is the ultimate Revelation to us from God, and in learning about who Jesus is, the students will also learn who he calls them to be.

prerequisites.raw: 9th grade Theology

courses.description: Semester 1 (The Paschal Mystery): The purpose of this course is to help students understand all that God has done for us through his Son, Jesus Christ. Students will learn that for all eternity God has planned for us to share eternal happiness with him, accomplished through the redemption Christ won for us, and that they share in this redemption only in and through Jesus Christ. They will also be introduced to what it means to be a disciple of Christ. Semester 2 (Ecclesiology): The purpose of this course is to help students understand that in and through the Church they encounter the living Jesus Christ. They will be introduced to the fact that the Church was founded by Christ through the Apostles and is sustained by him through the Holy Spirit, and will come to know the Church as the living Body of Christ today, with both divine and human elements.

courses.title: 2-D Studio Art I

courses.title: 2-D Studio Art II

courses.title: 3-D Sculpture

courses.title: Creative Photography

Students learn how to transform and enhance their photographs with photo-editing software, and view, discuss, critique, and reflect on the work of professional photographers. Students leave this course with a portfolio of digital photography that demonstrates the spectrum of techniques explored.

courses.title: Yearbook I
notes: This course meets the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.
courses.description: The purpose of this course is to enable students to extend fundamental skills in the production of journalism across print, multimedia, web, and broadcast/radio platforms and to acquire knowledge of journalism history, ethics, and management techniques related to the production of journalistic media.

courses.title: Drumming Techniques I

Performance techniques, music knowledge, critical analysis, and aesthetic response are emphasized.

Public performances may serve as a culmination of specific instructional goals.

courses.title: Instrumental Ensemble
notes: This course meets the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.

Public performances may serve as a culmination of specific instructional goals.

courses.title: Band I
notes: This course meets the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.

courses.title: Music Technology and Sound Engineering I
notes: This course meets the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.

Public performances may serve as a resource for specific instructional goals.

courses.title: Keyboard I (Piano Techniques)

Public performances may serve as a culmination of specific instructional goals.

courses.title: Guitar I

courses.title: Introduction to Drama

In keeping with the rigor expected in an accelerated setting, students assemble a portfolio that showcases a significant body of work representing personal vision and artistic growth over time; mastery of theatre skills and techniques in one or more areas; and evidence of significant oral and written analytical and problem-solving skills based on their structural, historical, and cultural knowledge.

Students participate and practice debates and drills in preparation for competitive debate.

courses.title: Foundations of Robotics Honors
notes: This course meets the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.

The objective of this course is to introduce students to the basic concepts of robot design and programming using the VEX V5 robotics system. Students work in teams to design, build, and test increasingly more complex robots, and apply what they have learned through a series of exciting and challenging robot competitions.

Hands-on activities using an entry-level game development tool such as Game Maker are integrated into the curriculum, and the culminating activity is the creation of a playable game.

Students may collaborate and share their solutions with their peers, and use components such as LEDs, diodes, and resistors in their circuitry.

courses.title: Multimedia Technologies

Students extend their knowledge of microprocessors with communications, analog and digital transmission, and interfacing with other microcontrollers and sensors. Communication may include Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and network protocols. Students use passive and/or active components in their circuitry, and in groups create a capstone project that focuses on a current issue.

courses.title: Communications Systems I

The ultimate output of this course is a design portfolio created by the student. Each item or product included in the portfolio should include a narrative description and an explanation of the technical approach or techniques used to create the item.

courses.title: Business & Entrepreneurship Principles Honors
notes: This course meets the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.
courses.description: This is a survey course in the principles underlying the management of all types of organizations, including objectives, policies, organization structure, coordination, control procedures, and environmental issues. Case studies are used extensively.

courses.title: Finance and Business Technology Honors

courses.description: The main purpose of this course is to provide practical and generic financial skills regarding money management, wise credit decisions, saving and investing money, and wise use of consumer protection agencies. The content is designed to enable students to demonstrate proficiency in practical financial management activities, use of a calculator in everyday living situations, and the performance of selected generic skills used in general business procedures.

This is a comprehensive course of study that includes, but is not limited to, classroom lectures, hands-on lab activities, and ambulance/fire rescue rides. This course also helps prepare students for other healthcare fields and is a prerequisite for paramedic training.

courses.title: Advanced Placement Computer Science Principles

prerequisites.raw: 3.50 GPA; 80+ in Algebra I Honors

notes: AP form due at Course Selection
Additional fee
This general elective course does not meet the Practical / Fine Arts requirement.

In this course, students develop computational thinking skills vital for success across all disciplines, such as using computational tools to analyze and study data, and working with large data sets to analyze, visualize, and draw conclusions from trends. The course engages students in the creative aspects of the field by allowing them to develop computational artifacts based on their interests. Students also develop effective communication and collaboration skills by working individually and collaboratively to solve problems, and discuss and write about the impacts these solutions could have on their community, society, and the world.

The guide's notes for AP Statistics, AP Psychology, and AP Computer Science Principles say students would 'choose a different math course' if minimum enrollment is not met; for the non-math courses this appears to be a copy-paste artifact in the source and is recorded here as 'a different course'.

Migrated from curriculum schema 1.0 to 2.0. `guide` became `document` with a `document_type`; `source_document` became the one-entry `source_documents` array; each course gained `department_canonical`, `credits_basis`, `source_refs` and the course-card fields, which are empty here because a narrative guide does not use footnote symbols.

Where a course lists more than one prerequisite, the cards mean any one of them — every such line in this catalog is a course and its honours or double-block twin. Those lines carry `prerequisites.choice: true` so the explorer treats them as a choice rather than demanding all of them.
